lessons.title: Planning a weekly cassava bread baking schedule
lessons.body: To scale up, you need a weekly schedule that matches demand and avoids waste. Start by tracking your sales for two weeks. If you sell 20 loaves on weekdays and 50 on weekends, plan to bake 25 on Monday, 25 on Tuesday, 30 on Wednesday, 30 on Thursday, 60 on Friday, and 70 on Saturday. Sunday is for rest and cleaning. Write this on a chalkboard or notebook. Your baking day starts the night before: soak cassava flour? No, cassava bread uses fresh or frozen grated cassava. Soak and press the cassava the day before. For 25 loaves, you need about 15 kg of fresh cassava roots. Peel, wash, and grate them in the afternoon. Then press out excess water using a screw press or heavy stones for 4-6 hours. In the evening, mix the dough with salt, oil, and any add-ins like onions or spices. Let it rest overnight in a cool place. The next morning, start baking at 5 AM. Use a wood-fired oven or a large drum oven. Bake in batches of 10 loaves for 45 minutes each. While one batch bakes, shape the next. By 10 AM, you should have all loaves ready for sale. Deliver to shops or sell at your stall. Clean up by noon. On Friday, double the batch for the weekend rush. Keep a calendar with orders marked. If a customer orders 100 loaves for a wedding, adjust your schedule and buy extra cassava. Always have 10% extra ingredients for mistakes. This rhythm builds trust and steady income.

lessons.title: Buying cassava in bulk from farmers
lessons.body: Buying cassava in bulk saves money and ensures supply. Find local farmers within 50 km. Visit during harvest season, which varies: in West Africa, cassava is ready 9-12 months after planting. Ask for a price per 50 kg bag. A fair price might be $10-$15 per bag. If you buy 20 bags, negotiate down to $8-$10. Always inspect the roots: they should be firm, no soft spots, no mold. Cut one open to check for white flesh and no brown streaks. Buy from at least two farmers to avoid shortages. Arrange transport: a pickup truck can carry 20 bags. If you don't have a vehicle, hire a taxi or use a motorcycle with a trailer. Pay half upfront, half on delivery. When the cassava arrives, process it within 24 hours to avoid spoilage. Grate and press immediately, or freeze the grated cassava in airtight bags for up to 3 months. For a weekly production of 100 loaves, you need about 60 kg of fresh cassava per week. That's 4-5 bags. Buy 20 bags monthly to get a discount. Store bags in a cool, dark room with good ventilation. Stack on pallets to prevent moisture. Check weekly for rot. If you see any, remove affected roots. Consider forming a buying group with other bakers to get even lower prices. This way, you control quality and cost.

lessons.title: Organizing a small bakery workspace
lessons.body: A well-organized workspace saves time and prevents accidents. Your bakery should have four zones: receiving, processing, baking, and packing. The receiving zone is near the door: a table for weighing and inspecting cassava. Next, the processing zone has a grater, press, and large mixing bowls. Keep a water source nearby. The baking zone has your oven and a cooling rack. The packing zone has a table, bags, and labels. Arrange them in a line so you don't cross paths. For a small bakery, a 4m x 6m room is enough. Use shelves on walls for tools. Label everything: 'grater', 'press', 'mixing bowls'. Keep a fire extinguisher and first aid kit. Floor should be concrete, easy to sweep. Good lighting and ventilation are key. Install a chimney for the oven. Have a handwashing station with soap and water. Store ingredients in sealed containers: cassava flour in bins, salt in jars. Keep a clipboard with daily tasks. At the end of each day, clean all surfaces with hot water and vinegar. This prevents mold and pests. A tidy workspace means faster production and happier workers. Invest in a stainless steel table if you can afford it; it's easy to sanitize. Otherwise, use wooden tables covered with plastic sheets. Keep a trash bin with a lid for peels. Empty it daily to avoid flies. With this setup, you can produce 50 loaves a day with two helpers.

lessons.title: Training and managing one or two helpers
lessons.body: When you hire helpers, train them properly. Start with one helper for every 20 loaves per day. Pay a fair daily wage: $5-$10 depending on your area. Train on the first day: show them how to peel cassava without waste. Use a sharp knife, cut off ends, slice skin lengthwise, and remove. Then teach grating: use a manual grater or a motorized one. Show the right pressure to avoid injury. Next, pressing: fill the press bag, tighten slowly. Then mixing: measure 5 kg grated cassava, 1 teaspoon salt, 2 tablespoons oil. Mix for 5 minutes. Finally, baking: preheat oven to 180Â°C, bake for 45 minutes. Let them watch you once, then do it under your supervision. Give clear instructions: 'Peel 10 kg', 'Grate 5 kg'. Check their work every hour. Praise good work, correct mistakes gently. Set rules: no phones during work, wash hands before handling food. Have a daily 10-minute meeting to plan. If you have two helpers, assign one to processing and one to baking. Rotate tasks weekly so they learn all steps. Pay on time. Provide one meal and clean water. Treat them with respect. If they are sick, let them rest. Keep a simple attendance book. After one month, increase pay if they are reliable. This builds loyalty and reduces turnover. Remember, a trained helper can run the bakery when you are away. That is true scaling.

lessons.title: Tracking ingredients and production costs
lessons.body: To make a profit, you must know your costs. Use a notebook or a simple spreadsheet. For each baking day, record: cassava (kg), salt (g), oil (ml), firewood or gas, and packaging. Also record labor and transport. For example, to make 20 loaves: 12 kg cassava at $0.50/kg = $6.00; salt $0.10; oil $0.50; firewood $2.00; bags $0.50; labor $5.00. Total cost = $14.10. If you sell each loaf for $1.00, revenue = $20.00. Profit = $5.90. That's a 42% margin. Track daily. At the end of the week, add all costs and revenues. Identify where you can save: buy cassava in bulk, use a more efficient oven, reduce waste. Keep a separate record for each recipe. If you add onions, note the extra cost. Also track your time: if you spend 6 hours, your labor is worth something. Even if you don't pay yourself, calculate it to know true cost. Use a simple formula: Cost per loaf = total cost / number of loaves. Then set your price to at least double that. Review monthly. If cassava prices rise, adjust your selling price or find a cheaper source. This tracking helps you make decisions: should you buy a motorized grater? If it saves 2 hours a day, yes. Keep receipts in an envelope. At the end of the month, you will see patterns and can plan better.

lessons.title: Avoiding common mistakes when doubling recipes
lessons.body: Doubling a recipe is not just multiplying everything by two. Common mistakes: adding too much liquid, overmixing, and wrong pan size. When you double cassava bread, the ratio of wet to dry changes because cassava releases water. For a single recipe of 2 kg grated cassava, you add 1 teaspoon salt and 2 tablespoons oil. For double (4 kg), add 1.5 teaspoons salt and 3 tablespoons oil, not 2 and 4. Why? Because salt and oil can overpower. Also, mixing takes longer: mix for 8 minutes instead of 5. If you use a wooden spoon, your arm will tire. Use a heavy-duty mixer or share the work. Baking time increases: a double batch in one oven may need 55-60 minutes, not 45. But if you bake in two pans, keep the same time. Never crowd the oven; air must circulate. Another mistake: not preheating long enough. For double, preheat 30 minutes. Also, check your oven's capacity. A small drum oven may only hold 10 loaves at a time. So doubling means two batches, not one giant batch. Keep notes: write down what worked. If you double and the bread is soggy, next time reduce water or press cassava longer. Always taste a small piece before baking the full batch. Adjust spices. Finally, don't double everything at once. Increase by 50% first, then 100%. This gradual approach prevents waste. With practice, you will master scaling.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Scaling Up Cassava Bread Production

This reference module is written for the small African bakery owner or cooperative baker who has moved beyond test batches and now needs to produce cassava bread consistently, profitably, and safely. It assumes you already know the basic cassava bread process â grating or milling cassava, pressing or dewatering, sieving, mixing with binders and other flours, shaping, and baking. The challenge at this stage is not the recipe itself. It is the system around the recipe: scheduling, sourcing, workspace design, helpers, costing, and the discipline to avoid mistakes that quietly destroy margins.

Across Nigeria, Ghana, Cameroon, Uganda, Kenya, and Tanzania, cassava bread enterprises often fail not because the bread is bad, but because production is chaotic. Bakers buy cassava when they remember, bake when orders come, guess at costs, and train helpers by shouting instructions during a rush. Scaling up requires turning those habits into routines. This module gives you the practical tools to do that.

1. Planning a Weekly Cassava Bread Baking Schedule

A weekly schedule is the backbone of scaling. It tells you when to buy, when to process cassava, when to bake, and when to sell. Without it, you will either overproduce and waste, or underproduce and lose customers.

Start by mapping your sales pattern. In most African markets, cassava bread sells best in the morning and early evening. Institutional buyers â schools, hospitals, hotels, and caterers â often order on specific days. Retail shops may need delivery twice a week. Your schedule should match these rhythms.

A practical weekly cycle for a small bakery producing 200â500 loaves per week might look like this: Monday for bulk cassava purchase and quality checks; Tuesday for processing and dough preparation; Wednesday for baking and retail delivery; Thursday for institutional orders; Friday for a second baking cycle and weekend stock; Saturday for market sales; Sunday for cleaning, maintenance, and cost review.

The key is to separate cassava processing from baking days. Fresh cassava must be processed quickly after harvest â usually within 24â48 hours â to avoid spoilage and cyanogenic risk. If you buy on Monday, you should process by Tuesday. Baking can follow immediately or the next day, depending on your fermentation or resting method.

2. Buying Cassava in Bulk from Farmers

Bulk buying lowers your unit cost and gives you more control over quality, but only if you do it properly. The biggest mistake small bakers make is buying from the nearest farmer without checking variety, age, or cyanogenic potential. Some cassava varieties are sweet and low in cyanogenic compounds; others are bitter and require longer processing. For bread, you want consistent, mature roots with high dry matter and low bitterness.

Build relationships with two or three reliable farmers rather than one. This protects you against crop failure, price spikes, and transport problems. Agree on a buying calendar that matches your weekly schedule. If you buy every Monday, farmers can harvest on Sunday and deliver fresh roots on Monday morning.

Always inspect roots before payment. Look for firmness, absence of rot, no soft spots, and uniform size. Reject roots that are bruised, moldy, or unusually bitter. If possible, test a small batch before committing to a large purchase. In many African markets, cassava is sold by heap, basin, or kilogram. Move to kilogram-based pricing as soon as possible because it makes costing accurate.

Table 1: Bulk cassava buying checklist for small bakeries
Factor Good Practice Why It Matters
Variety Buy known sweet or low-cyanogenic varieties suitable for flour Reduces processing time and safety risk
Freshness Roots harvested within 24â48 hours Fresh roots have better starch and less spoilage
Price basis Buy by kilogram or standardized weight Enables accurate cost tracking and fair pricing
Supplier number Use at least two farmers Reduces risk of shortage or price manipulation
Transport Use clean, covered transport Prevents contamination and bruising
Payment terms Agree clearly: cash, mobile money, or weekly settlement Builds trust and reliable supply

Source: Compiled from FAO cassava market guidance and IITA post-harvest handling recommendations.

3. Organizing a Small Bakery Workspace

Scaling up does not require a large building. It requires a logical flow. Your workspace should move raw cassava in one direction and finished bread out the other, with no crossing between dirty and clean zones. This reduces contamination and makes training helpers easier.

Divide your workspace into five zones: receiving and storage, washing and peeling, grating or milling, pressing and sieving, and baking and cooling. If possible, keep a separate area for packing and sales. In many African bakeries, the same table is used for everything. That is a hidden cost because it slows production and increases the risk of spoilage.

Invest in simple improvements: raised work tables, covered bins, clean water containers, a dedicated press or dewatering system, and labeled storage containers for flour, binders, salt, sugar, and yeast. Good lighting and ventilation are not luxuries; they improve speed and safety.

4. Training and Managing One or Two Helpers

Your first helpers should be people who can follow instructions, arrive on time, and handle food safely. Train them on specific tasks, not vague responsibilities. For example, one helper can handle washing, peeling, and grating. Another can handle pressing, sieving, and packing. You focus on mixing, baking, quality control, and sales.

Write down the steps for each task. Even a simple handwritten card on the wall helps. Demonstrate once, let the helper do it while you watch, then correct gently. Repeat until consistent. Pay fairly and on time. In many African contexts, reliable pay and respect reduce turnover more than high wages alone.

Hold a short daily check-in before production starts. Confirm the day's target, who does what, and any quality issues from the previous batch. Keep a simple attendance and task sheet. This is not bureaucracy; it is how you protect your brand.

5. Tracking Ingredients and Production Costs

If you do not know your cost per loaf, you cannot price confidently or grow sustainably. Track every ingredient and every overhead item. Cassava flour, wheat or other binder flour, yeast, salt, sugar, oil, packaging, fuel, water, transport, and labor all count.

Use a simple notebook or a mobile spreadsheet. Record the quantity purchased, unit cost, and date. At the end of each baking day, record the number of loaves produced and sold. Divide total cost by number of loaves to get your cost per loaf. Add your target profit margin to set your selling price.

Table 2: Example weekly cost tracking sheet for cassava bread production
Cost Item Quantity Used Unit Cost (Local Currency) Total Cost Notes
Fresh cassava 200 kg â â Record actual price per kg
Binder flour 20 kg â â Wheat, sorghum, or composite
Yeast 1 kg â â Check expiry date
Salt and sugar 2 kg â â Record separately
Packaging 300 bags â â Include labels if used
Fuel or firewood â â â Track oven energy
Labor â â â Daily or weekly wages
Transport â â â Cassava and delivery
Total Weekly Cost â â â Divide by loaves produced

Source: Adapted from FAO/WHO small-scale food enterprise costing guidance and common African bakery practice.

6. Avoiding Common Mistakes When Doubling Recipes

Doubling a cassava bread recipe is not simply multiplying every ingredient by two. Cassava dough behaves differently at scale. It absorbs water differently, ferments faster or slower depending on temperature, and can become difficult to handle if the binder ratio is wrong.

Common mistakes include adding too much water at once, overmixing, using old yeast, skipping the resting time, and baking at the same temperature for the same time as a small batch. Larger batches need more even mixing and sometimes longer baking at slightly lower heat. Always test a small portion of the doubled dough before baking the entire batch.

â  SAFETY WARNING: Cassava Cyanide and Food Safety

Raw cassava contains cyanogenic glycosides. Improper processing can leave dangerous levels of cyanide in flour and bread. Never skip grating, pressing, soaking, drying, or fermentation steps. Never use bitter cassava without extended processing. Never sell or eat bread made from under-processed cassava. When in doubt, process longer, dry thoroughly, and test a small batch. Cyanide poisoning can cause dizziness, vomiting, weakness, and in severe cases death. Follow national food safety guidelines and work with extension officers or qualified food technologists.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Plan your week: separate buying, processing, baking, and selling days.
  • Buy cassava from at least two reliable farmers and inspect every batch.
  • Process fresh cassava within 24â48 hours of purchase.
  • Organize your workspace into clean and dirty zones with one-way flow.
  • Train helpers on specific tasks and write down each step.
  • Track every ingredient and overhead cost in a simple notebook or phone.
  • Calculate cost per loaf before setting your selling price.
  • When doubling recipes, adjust water, mixing time, and baking temperature carefully.
  • Never compromise on cassava processing safety.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Cassava: A Guide to Production, Processing and Utilisation
  • IITA â Cassava Research and Post-Harvest Handling
  • FAO â Food Loss and Waste Reduction
  • WHO â Natural Toxins in Food: Cyanogenic Glycosides
  • IFPRI â Cassava Value Chain and Market Research

Business-first reminder: Scaling up is not about baking more. It is about building a repeatable system that protects quality, controls cost, and keeps customers coming back. Master the schedule, the sourcing, the workspace, the team, and the numbers. The bread will follow.

quiz.q: What is the first step in planning a weekly cassava bread baking schedule?
options: B) Track your sales for two weeks
quiz.explanation: Tracking sales helps you match production to demand.

quiz.q: How many kilograms of fresh cassava roots are needed for 25 loaves?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states that for 25 loaves, you need about 15 kg of fresh cassava roots.

quiz.q: When should you start baking on a baking day?
quiz.explanation: Starting at 5 AM allows you to finish by 10 AM for sales.

quiz.q: What is a fair price range for a 50 kg bag of cassava when buying in bulk?
quiz.explanation: The lesson suggests a fair price is $10-$15 per 50 kg bag.

quiz.q: How soon should you process fresh cassava after buying?
quiz.explanation: Processing within 24 hours prevents spoilage.

quiz.q: What is a good way to store grated cassava for later use?
options: A) Leave it in the sun
C) Keep in an open bowl
quiz.explanation: Freezing grated cassava in airtight bags preserves it for up to 3 months.

quiz.q: How many zones should a small bakery workspace have?
quiz.explanation: The lesson describes four zones: receiving, processing, baking, and packing.

quiz.q: What is the recommended size for a small bakery room?
quiz.explanation: A 4m x 6m room is enough for a small bakery.

quiz.q: Why should you label tools and containers in the bakery?
options: B) To save time and prevent mistakes
quiz.explanation: Labeling helps workers find tools quickly and avoid mix-ups.

quiz.q: What should you use to clean surfaces daily?
quiz.explanation: Hot water and vinegar clean effectively and prevent mold.

quiz.q: How many helpers should you start with for 20 loaves per day?
quiz.explanation: The lesson suggests one helper for every 20 loaves per day.

quiz.q: What is a fair daily wage for a helper?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states a fair daily wage is $5-$10 depending on the area.

quiz.q: What should you do after training a helper on a task?
options: B) Supervise and check their work
D) Give them a day off
quiz.explanation: Supervising ensures they do the task correctly and safely.

quiz.q: How often should you rotate tasks if you have two helpers?
quiz.explanation: Rotating weekly helps helpers learn all steps.

quiz.q: What is a good practice to build loyalty among helpers?
options: B) Provide meals and clean water
quiz.explanation: Providing meals and clean water shows respect and builds loyalty.

quiz.q: What should you record to track ingredients and production costs?
options: B) Cassava, salt, oil, firewood, packaging, labor, transport
quiz.explanation: Recording all ingredients and costs gives a true picture of expenses.

quiz.q: If you sell 20 loaves for $1 each and total cost is $14.10, what is your profit?
quiz.explanation: Profit = revenue ($20) - cost ($14.10) = $5.90.

quiz.q: What is the formula for cost per loaf?
options: A) Total cost / number of loaves
B) Number of loaves / total cost
C) Total cost x number of loaves
D) Total cost + number of loaves
quiz.explanation: Cost per loaf is total cost divided by number of loaves.

quiz.q: Why should you calculate your own labor cost even if you don't pay yourself?
options: A) To know true cost and set price
quiz.explanation: Including labor gives the true cost, helping you set a profitable price.

quiz.q: How often should you review your cost tracking?
quiz.explanation: Monthly review helps you see patterns and adjust.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when doubling a cassava bread recipe?
options: B) Using the same pan size
quiz.explanation: Doubling can lead to too much liquid because cassava releases water.

quiz.q: For a double batch of 4 kg grated cassava, how much salt should you add?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says to add 1.5 teaspoons of salt, not double the original.

quiz.q: How long should you mix a double batch of cassava dough?
quiz.explanation: Mixing takes longer for a double batch: about 8 minutes.

quiz.q: If you bake a double batch in one oven, how long should it bake?
quiz.explanation: A double batch in one oven needs 55-60 minutes.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid crowding the oven when doubling?
options: B) Air must circulate for even baking
D) It makes the bread too brown
quiz.explanation: Crowding prevents air circulation, leading to uneven baking.

quiz.q: What is a safe way to increase recipe size?
quiz.explanation: Gradual increase prevents waste and mistakes.

quiz.q: What should you do before baking a full double batch?
quiz.explanation: Tasting a small piece allows you to adjust seasoning.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep notes when scaling recipes?
quiz.explanation: Notes help you repeat successes and avoid past mistakes.

quiz.q: What is a sign that you may have added too much water when doubling?
options: B) The bread is too hard
C) The bread is too salty
D) The bread is too small
quiz.explanation: Too much water makes the bread soggy.

quiz.q: What should you do if your oven only holds 10 loaves but you need to bake 20?
quiz.explanation: Baking in two batches is the practical solution for limited oven capacity.
